The course is organized into six sequential modules that build on one another. Total
pacing is approximately 12--14 weeks, consistent with a standard semester.
\begin{center}

\toprule
\textbf{\#} & \textbf{Module} & \textbf{Duration} & \textbf{Syllabus \S\S} \\
\midrule

1 & Review of Basic Properties of Functions & 2$^-$ weeks & Ch.\,1, 2.1--2.2 \\
2 & Limits and Continuity & 2 weeks & 3.1--3.5 \\
3 & Derivatives & 3$^-$ weeks & 4.1--4.11 \\
4 & Applications of Differentiation & 2$^+$ weeks & 5.1--5.5 \\
5 & Integration & 2 weeks & 5.10, 6.1--6.3 \\
6 & Applications of the Integral & 1$^+$ week & 7.1--7.3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{center}
\noindent\textbf{Overall course prerequisite (entry-level).} Solid precalculus /
college algebra \& trigonometry: function notation and graphing, exponent and
logarithm rules, trigonometric identities and the unit circle, polynomial
factoring, and algebraic manipulation of rational expressions. These are assumed
on day one and are only briefly reviewed in Module 1.
\noindent\textbf{Course-level learning arc.} Functions $\rightarrow$ limiting behavior
$\rightarrow$ instantaneous rate of change (derivatives) $\rightarrow$ using derivatives
to analyze behavior $\rightarrow$ accumulation (integrals) $\rightarrow$ techniques to
evaluate integrals. Each module is the conceptual prerequisite for the next.

mod:1 Module 1 --- Functions, Exponential Growth & Decay, Sequences (2^- weeks) Chapters/Sections: Chapter 1 --- Preliminaries: functions, domain/range, function types, graph transformations, composition and inverses 2.1 --- Exponential Growth and Decay 2.2 --- Sequences Core Concepts: Function definitions: polynomial, rational, power, trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, piecewise Domain, range, and graphical behavior; even/odd symmetry; increasing/decreasing behavior Composition of functions and inverse functions Exponential models N(t) = N_0 e^kt; growth vs.\ decay; doubling time and half-life Sequences: explicit vs.\ recursive definitions; convergence, divergence, and limits of a sequence \loheader Classify a function by type and determine its domain and range algebraically and graphically Compose and invert functions, and interpret inverses in applied contexts Construct exponential growth/decay models from word problems and solve for rate, time, or initial quantity Compute and interpret half-life and doubling time Determine whether a sequence converges or diverges, and find its limit when it exists Translating a word problem into an exponential model (identifying N_0 and k correctly, including sign of k) Distinguishing sequence convergence from the behavior of a related continuous function Working fluently with logarithm and exponent rules under time pressure Algebra I/II: function notation, graphing, solving equations. Precalculus: exponent and logarithm laws, interpreting graphs of e^x and \ln x.

mod:2 Module 2 --- Limits, Continuity, and Limiting Behavior (2 weeks) Chapters/Sections: 3.1 --- Limits (intuitive approach, with the formal \varepsilon--\delta definition introduced via 3.6) 3.2 --- Continuity 3.3 --- Limits at Infinity (with the formal definition via 3.6) 3.4 --- Trigonometric Limits and the Sandwich (Squeeze) Theorem 3.5 --- Properties of Continuous Functions Core Concepts: One-sided and two-sided limits; limit laws Formal \varepsilon--\delta definition of a limit Continuity at a point and on an interval; types of discontinuities (removable, jump, infinite) Horizontal/vertical asymptotes and limits at infinity Squeeze (Sandwich) Theorem, especially applied to \lim_\theta \to 0\frac\sin\theta\theta Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) and Extreme Value Theorem groundwork \loheader Evaluate limits algebraically (factoring, rationalizing), graphically, and numerically Write and interpret an \varepsilon--\delta proof for a simple limit statement Classify discontinuities and determine continuity of piecewise functions Evaluate limits at infinity and identify horizontal/vertical asymptotes Apply the Squeeze Theorem to evaluate trigonometric limits Apply the IVT to justify the existence of roots or solutions The formal \varepsilon--\delta definition: translating a symbolic statement into a working proof Indeterminate forms (0/0, \infty - \infty) requiring algebraic manipulation before a limit can be evaluated Recognizing when/how to apply the Squeeze Theorem rather than direct substitution Distinguishing a removable discontinuity from a true break in continuity Module 1 (function behavior, graphing). Algebraic fluency: factoring, rationalizing radicals, trigonometric identities.

\begin{modulebox}{Module 3 --- Differentiation Rules and Techniques \hfill (3$^-$ weeks)}
\textbf{Chapters/Sections:}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item 4.1 --- Formal Definition of the Derivative
  \item 4.2 --- Basic Rules of Derivatives
  \item 4.3 --- Power Rule and the Rules of Differentiation
  \item 4.4 --- Product and Quotient Rules
  \item 4.5 --- The Chain Rule
  \item 4.6 --- Implicit Functions and Implicit Differentiation
  \item 4.7 --- Higher Derivatives
  \item 4.8 --- Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
  \item 4.9 --- Derivatives of Exponential Functions
  \item 4.10 --- Derivatives of Inverse Functions
  \item 4.11 --- Linear Approximation
\end{itemize}
\textbf{Core Concepts:}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item Derivative as a limit of a difference quotient; derivative as instantaneous rate of change and slope of tangent line
  \item Differentiability vs.\ continuity
  \item Sum, constant multiple, power, product, quotient, and chain rules
  \item Implicit differentiation for curves not expressed as $y = f(x)$
  \item Second and higher-order derivatives; notation ($f''$, $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$)
  \item Derivatives of $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $\tan x$, $e^x$, and inverse functions (including logarithmic and inverse trig)
  \item Linear approximation / tangent line approximation, $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$
\end{itemize}
\loheader
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item Compute a derivative directly from the limit definition
  \item Apply the power, product, quotient, and chain rules fluently, including in combination
  \item Perform implicit differentiation and find slopes of tangent lines to implicit curves
  \item Compute higher-order derivatives and interpret their meaning (e.g., concavity, acceleration)
  \item Differentiate trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, and inverse functions
  \item Use linear approximation to estimate function values near a point
\end{itemize}
\end{modulebox}

\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{0. Course Overview}
The source textbook covers twelve chapters that blend standard single- and
multivariable calculus with discrete-time modeling, differential equations,
linear algebra, and probability/statistics --- the toolkit most commonly used
in biology and social-science quantitative courses. Twelve chapters is more
material than a single semester of ``Calculus 1'' typically covers, so this
breakdown makes the following working assumption, stated here explicitly:
\begin{quote}\small
\textbf{Assumption.} The textbook is delivered across a two-semester sequence.
\textbf{Calculus I} (this course) corresponds to \textbf{Chapters 1--6}
(precalculus review through integration). \textbf{Calculus II} corresponds to
\textbf{Chapters 7--12} (integration techniques through probability and
statistics) and is included here so the breakdown reflects the complete table
of contents and shows how Calculus I feeds into it. If your program instead
runs this material as a single accelerated semester, a three-quarter sequence,
or omits later chapters, the six modules below can be regrouped or trimmed
without changing their internal structure.
\end{quote}
\paragraph{Audience and emphasis} Students are primarily biology, ecology,
pre-health, and social-science majors. Motivating examples throughout the
course are drawn from population growth, drug kinetics, epidemiology,
ecological interactions, demography, and data analysis rather than physics.
\paragraph{Asterisk convention} Following the textbook's own convention,
topics marked with an asterisk (*) are optional or enrichment material --
deeper rigor (e.g.\ formal $\varepsilon$--$\delta$ limits), extensions of core
ideas (e.g.\ stability of recurrence equations), or additional modeling
examples. A course can be taught in full without covering starred topics;
instructors choose which to include based on time and student background.
\paragraph{Computational component} Several sections (numerical recursion,
the bisection method, numerical integration) are built around spreadsheet
use. A weekly computer lab or homework component using a spreadsheet
application is recommended alongside lecture.

\item \textbf{Complex numbers:} arithmetic of complex numbers and the
quadratic formula for non-real roots.
\end{itemize}

the list above are expected to be identified and remediated in the first two
weeks rather than assumed away.

\MajorTopics
\begin{itemize}
\item Precalculus skills diagnostic test
\item Preliminaries: real numbers, lines, circles, trigonometry, exponentials/logarithms, complex numbers and quadratics
\item Elementary functions: polynomial, rational, power, exponential, inverse, logarithmic, trigonometric
\item Graphing: transformations, logarithmic scales, transforming data into linear form, (optional) verbal description to graph
\end{itemize}
\KeyConcepts
Function families and their defining properties; domain/range; graph
transformations (shifts, stretches, reflections); inverse functions;
logarithmic and semi-log axes as a way to linearize exponential or
power-law data.
\LearnObj
\begin{enumerate}
\item Use the diagnostic test to identify and remediate personal precalculus gaps.
\item Solve equations involving lines, circles, exponentials, logarithms, and quadratics (including non-real roots).
\item Classify a function by family and describe its domain, range, and key graphical features.
\item Apply shifts, stretches, and reflections to graph a function and its inverse.
\item Re-express exponential or power-law data on logarithmic or semi-log axes to reveal a linear trend.
\item * Translate a verbal description of a process into a qualitative graph.
\end{enumerate}
\PreReq High-school algebra, geometry, and trigonometry (see Section 1 above).
\Hard Complex numbers and the quadratic formula tend to be rusty for
returning students; log and semi-log scales are conceptually new even to
students comfortable with logarithms as a computation. Building a
qualitative graph directly from a verbal story (Sec.\ 1.4.4*) is a skill,
not a formula, and benefits from in-class modeling.

\MajorTopics
\begin{itemize}
\item Exponential growth and decay: discrete-time population models, recurrence equations, visualization
\item Sequences: definitions, (optional) spreadsheet calculation, limits, recurrence equations, sigma notation
\item Modeling with recurrence equations: density-dependent growth, the Beverton--Holt model, the discrete logistic equation, (optional) drug absorption
\end{itemize}
\KeyConcepts
Recurrence (difference) equations; discrete exponential growth
$N_{t+1}=RN_t$; cobweb/stair-step diagrams; convergence of a sequence;
sigma notation; density dependence and carrying capacity; the
Beverton--Holt and discrete logistic maps.
\LearnObj
\begin{enumerate}
\item Formulate a recurrence equation that models discrete-time population growth or decay.
\item Iterate and visualize solutions of a recurrence equation using cobweb/stair-step diagrams.
\item Determine whether a sequence converges and, if so, find its limit.
\item Evaluate sums of sequences using sigma notation.
\item Compare density-independent and density-dependent growth models and interpret carrying capacity.
\item * Model drug absorption using a discrete recurrence equation.
\end{enumerate}
\PreReq Exponential and logarithmic functions (Sec.\ 1.3.5, 1.3.7); comfort with algebraic manipulation of equations.
\Hard Predicting the long-term (equilibrium or oscillatory) behavior of a
\emph{nonlinear} recurrence equation is the first genuinely modeling-heavy
task in the course and is often harder than the algebra itself; students
also frequently struggle to set up a recurrence equation directly from a

\begin{itemize}
\item Counting: the multiplication principle, permutations, combinations, combining the counting principles
\item What is probability? Basic definitions and equally likely outcomes
\item Conditional probability and independence: conditional probability, the Law of Total Probability, independence, the Bayes formula
\item Discrete random variables and discrete distributions: means and variances; the binomial, multinomial, geometric, and Poisson distributions
\item Continuous distributions: density functions, the normal, uniform, and exponential distributions, the Poisson process, aging
\item Limit theorems: the Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem
\item Statistical tools: describing univariate data, estimating parameters, linear regression
\end{itemize}
\KeyConcepts
Permutations and combinations; sample spaces and events; conditional
probability and independence; Bayes' Theorem; discrete random variables,
expectation, and variance; the binomial, geometric, and Poisson
distributions; probability density functions; the normal, uniform, and
exponential distributions; the Law of Large Numbers; the Central Limit
Theorem; point estimation; linear regression.
\LearnObj
\begin{enumerate}
\item Apply counting techniques (multiplication principle, permutations, combinations) to compute probabilities.
\item Compute conditional probabilities and apply the Law of Total Probability and Bayes' Theorem.
\item Work with discrete distributions (binomial, geometric, Poisson), including computing mean and variance.
\item Work with continuous probability distributions (normal, uniform, exponential), including computing probabilities by integrating density functions.
\item State and apply the Law of Large Numbers and the Central Limit Theorem.
\item Summarize univariate data, estimate distribution parameters, and fit a linear regression model.
\end{enumerate}
\PreReq Integration (Chapters 6--7), needed for continuous densities; counting and basic algebra (Chapter 1).

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Discrete-to-continuous transitions.} Students build strong
discrete-time intuition in Chapter 2, then must re-learn stability and
growth concepts in continuous form in Chapters 5 and 8. Explicitly
cross-referencing the discrete and continuous versions of the same idea
(e.g.\ discrete vs.\ continuous exponential growth, equilibrium stability
of a recurrence equation vs.\ an ODE) shortens this transition.
\item \textbf{Rigor vs.\ intuition.} The starred rigorous topics
($\varepsilon$--$\delta$ limits, the Riemann integral construction, the
Leibniz's Rule proof of the FTC) sit in tension with the course's
model-building emphasis. Treating them as optional deep dives, clearly
separated from the applied spine of the course, works better than
interleaving them.
\item \textbf{Word-problem translation.} Related rates, optimization,
compartment/epidemic modeling, and Leslie-matrix demography all share the
same underlying difficulty: converting a verbal description into equations
before any calculus or algebra is applied. This is best taught as an
explicit, repeated skill (define variables, state relationships, then
compute) rather than assumed.
\item \textbf{Stacked symbolic technique.} The chain rule combined with
implicit differentiation, and partial fractions combined with
substitution, both require executing several symbolic steps in the correct
order; errors compound quickly, so scaffolded, partial-credit practice
matters more here than in single-step computations.
\item \textbf{Eigenvalue-based qualitative reasoning.} Eigenvalues recur as
the organizing idea behind Leslie-matrix demography (Ch.\ 9), linear
systems of ODEs (Ch.\ 11), and linearization of nonlinear systems (Ch.\
10--11). Investing extra time in Sec.\ 9.3.2 pays off across the rest of
the second semester.
\item \textbf{Probabilistic reasoning.} Bayes' Theorem and the Central
Limit Theorem are conceptually distinct from the calculus that precedes
them and often need to be taught with less reliance on procedural fluency
and more reliance on worked examples and simulation.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Calculus for Biology and Medicine} (4th ed.) is written for a one- or two-semester
calculus sequence for life-science and social-science majors. Its twelve chapters run from
precalculus review through probability and statistics, and the authors explicitly design
sections marked with an asterisk (\opt) as optional ``instructor's choice'' material that
can be trimmed without breaking the logical flow of the book.
This document treats \textbf{Chapters 1--6} as \emph{Calculus 1}: precalculus review,
discrete-time (recurrence) models, limits and continuity, differentiation, applications of
differentiation, and integration through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. This mirrors
how the book is used in two-semester bio-calculus tracks (e.g., the first course covers
single-variable differential and integral calculus, and a second course, \emph{Calculus 2},
covers Chapters 7--12: integration techniques, differential equations, linear algebra,
multivariable calculus, systems of differential equations, and probability/statistics --
see Appendix~\ref{app:calc2}). Instructors on a one-semester-only track can compress the
schedule in Section~\ref{sec:schedule} by cutting all asterisked (\opt) subsections.
\textbf{Distinguishing feature of this course:} unlike a generic ``applied calculus''
course, every mathematical tool is introduced through a biological or social-science model
first (population growth, drug absorption and elimination, enzyme kinetics, epidemics,
allometric scaling, blood alcohol elimination, oxygen binding in blood) and only then
treated with full mathematical rigor. Word-problem literacy -- turning a verbal description
of a process into an equation -- is therefore treated as a first-class course objective,
not an afterthought.

By the end of the course, a successful student will be able to:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{SLO\arabic*.}, leftmargin=2.6em]
\item \textbf{Model discrete and continuous change.} Translate a verbal description of a
      biological or social process into a recurrence equation, a limit statement, a
      derivative, or a definite integral, and interpret the mathematical result back in
      the original context.
\item \textbf{Evaluate limits and determine continuity} of algebraic, exponential,
      logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, including limits at infinity and limits
      that require the sandwich theorem.
\item \textbf{Differentiate} elementary, polynomial, rational, power, exponential,
      logarithmic, and trigonometric functions using the formal definition and the rules
      of differentiation (sum, product, quotient, chain, implicit).
\item \textbf{Apply derivatives} to find extrema, analyze monotonicity and concavity,
      solve optimization and related-rates problems, evaluate indeterminate forms
      (L'H\^{o}pital's Rule), and produce derivative-informed graphs.
\item \textbf{Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals}, state and apply both parts of
      the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and interpret a definite integral as
      cumulative change or an average value.
\item \textbf{Use technology} (graphing calculators or spreadsheets) to visualize
      functions and data, iterate recurrence equations, and implement simple numerical
      methods (bisection, Newton--Raphson).
\item \textbf{Communicate quantitative reasoning}, including the assumptions behind a
      mathematical model, its limitations, and how well it fits real or simulated data.
\end{enumerate}

Formal prerequisite: a passing grade in Algebra II / Precalculus, or a satisfactory score
on a placement/diagnostic exam. Chapter 1 of the text (\S1.1--\S1.4) is built into Week 1--2
of the schedule as an explicit, graded review rather than an assumption, since incoming
preparation varies widely between life-science and social-science students. Students should
arrive able to:
\begin{itemize}
\item Perform algebraic manipulation of real numbers, absolute values, and inequalities.
\item Write the equation of a line (point--slope, slope--intercept, standard form) and a circle.
\item Convert between degrees and radians and recall basic trigonometric identities.
\item Apply the laws of exponents and logarithms; solve simple exponential/log equations.
\item Solve linear and quadratic equations, including via the quadratic formula.
\item Identify domain, range, and composition of a function from a formula or graph.
\item Recognize and sketch polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic,
      and trigonometric functions, and apply basic graph transformations.
\end{itemize}

independent of which module they fall in, together with a brief teaching strategy.
\begin{longtable}{P{1.4cm}P{4.3cm}P{9.4cm}}

\midrule
\endhead
1.4.3 & Linearizing data (log--log, semilog) & New use of logarithms (as a data-transformation tool, not just a function). Pair every algebra step with a plotted example. \\
2.2.3, 2.2.5 & Sequence limits \& $\Sigma$-notation & First rigorous limit idea and first heavy use of index notation; both recur constantly later. Over-invest time here. \\
2.3.3 & Discrete logistic map / chaos & Counter-intuitive: a simple deterministic rule can produce non-repeating output. Use live spreadsheet iteration to build intuition before discussing theory. \\
3.6\opt & $\varepsilon$--$\delta$ limit definition & Highly abstract quantifier logic ($\forall \varepsilon\, \exists \delta$). Optional -- skip or treat as enrichment unless rigor is a stated course goal. \\
4.5 & Chain rule (nested compositions) & Errors compound with each layer of composition. Practice ``outside-in'' peeling with 3+ layer examples. \\
4.6.2 & Related rates & Failure is usually at translation (setting up the equation), not differentiation. Require a labeled diagram before any calculus. \\
4.11 & Error propagation & Requires connecting linear approximation to a measurement-science idea (absolute vs.\ relative vs.\ percentage error) many students have not seen. \\
5.4 & Optimization word problems & Same translation bottleneck as related rates, plus justifying that a critical point is the desired extremum. Use a fixed 4-step template. \\
5.5 & L'H\^{o}pital's Rule & Commonly mis-applied to non-indeterminate forms. Require students to state the indeterminate form \emph{before} differentiating. \\
6.1.2 & Riemann sums / definite integral as a limit & Second ``limit of an infinite process'' idea; the output is a number, not a function, which confuses students expecting an antiderivative-style answer. \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

Math 617 is a first-semester graduate course in algebraic number theory. It assumes familiarity with graduate algebra and analysis at the qualifying-exam level and proceeds from the arithmetic of Dedekind domains through local and global fields to adèles and idèles, with Tate's thesis as an optional capstone topic if time permits. The course meets twice weekly (Tuesday/Thursday, 75 minutes) over a 15-week semester, with several sessions reserved for homework discussion. Grading is 100\% homework, assigned weekly, with one or two randomly-selected problems graded for accuracy and the remainder for completion; the lowest homework score is dropped.
This document expands the syllabus's four topic areas into a full breakdown: modules, chapters/reference correspondences, concepts, learning objectives, and difficult topics, together with the prerequisite background assumed at the outset.

\textbf{Topics.} Algebraic number fields and their rings of integers; Noetherian, integrally closed domains of Krull dimension~1; equivalent characterizations of a Dedekind domain; unique factorization of nonzero ideals into prime ideals; localization at a prime; fractional ideals; first look at the ideal class group.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item State and prove the equivalence of the standard characterizations of a Dedekind domain (Noetherian + integrally closed + dimension~1 $\iff$ every nonzero ideal factors uniquely into primes $\iff$ localizations are DVRs).
  \item Factor concrete ideals in rings of integers of quadratic and cyclotomic fields.
  \item Distinguish factorization of ideals from (nonunique) factorization of elements.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Number Theory I} is a two-semester (year-long) graduate sequence covering the foundations of algebraic number theory, the theory of local fields, the adelic/idelic reformulation of classical algebraic number theory, the analytic theory of zeta and $L$-functions, and local and global class field theory. The course is designed for students who have completed a first-year graduate algebra sequence and wish to specialize in number theory, arithmetic geometry, or representation theory.
The guiding philosophy is the \textbf{function-field analogy}: number fields behave like curves over finite fields, ideals like divisors, ramification like branching, and the Riemann--Roch theorem, zeta functions, and class field theory all express manifestations of a single underlying structure. Weil's adelic language is used throughout as the unifying framework, while Neukirch supplies the clearest linear exposition and Lang supplies the deepest analytic tools.

readable_text: Weeks 1--4 (Sessions 1--8). Goal: establish the ring-theoretic foundations --- Dedekind domains, ideal factorization, and ramification in extensions --- that underlie everything else in the course.

Core concepts Noetherian, integrally closed, Krull dimension one (every nonzero prime is maximal) Equivalent characterizations: localization at every prime is a DVR; every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible Examples: \OK for a number field K, coordinate rings of smooth affine curves, PIDs Non-example: non-maximal orders, e.g.\ \Z[\sqrt-3] Learning objectives Explain the equivalent characterizations of a Dedekind domain and prove their equivalence Derive that \OK is a Dedekind domain from integrality and finiteness properties Apply localization arguments to reduce global ring-theoretic questions to the DVR case Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show that a PID is a Dedekind domain. Rubric: PID \Rightarrow Noetherian (ACC on ideals); UFD \Rightarrow integrally closed; nonzero primes in a PID are generated by irreducibles, hence maximal. [Q2 (advanced).] Let A = \Z[\sqrt-3]. Exhibit an element of Frac(A) integral over A but not in A, and conclude A is not Dedekind. Answer: \tfrac1+\sqrt-32 satisfies x^2-x+1=0 and lies in O_\Q(\sqrt-3)=\Z[\tfrac1+\sqrt-32], but not in A.

Core concepts Fractional ideals and their group structure under multiplication Unique factorization of ideals into primes (existence and uniqueness) The ideal class group Cl(K) = fractional ideals modulo principal ideals Finiteness of Cl(K) (stated here; proved in Module 2 via Minkowski theory) Learning objectives Prove unique factorization of ideals in a Dedekind domain Compute the ideal class group in small examples Explain the relationship between class number one and unique factorization of elements Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show every nonzero fractional ideal of a Dedekind domain is invertible. Rubric: prove local invertibility at each prime using the DVR structure, then glue. [Q2 (advanced).] Compute Cl(\Q(\sqrt-5)) by exhibiting a non-principal ideal. Rubric: factor (2,1+\sqrt-5) as a prime above 2, show non-principal via a norm argument, show its square is principal; conclude Cl(K)\cong \Z/2.

Core concepts The integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite extension is again Dedekind Factorization p\OL = \prod P_i^e_i in an extension L/K The ideal norm and its multiplicativity Learning objectives Derive the factorization p\OL = \prod P_i^e_i from unique factorization Compute prime factorizations in specific number field extensions Apply the norm map to relate ideal factorization to field degree Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Factor (2) in \Z[i]. Answer: (2) = (1+i)^2, ramified since 2 \mid disc(\Q(i)). [Q2 (advanced).] Determine how 5 and 11 factor in \Q(\zeta_5). Rubric: 5 is totally ramified since 5\mid disc(\Q(\zeta_5)); the splitting of 11 is governed by the order of 11 mod 5.

Core concepts Definitions of ramification index e_i and residue degree f_i The fundamental identity \sum e_i f_i = [L:K]; constant e,f when L/K is Galois Split, inert, and ramified primes, with examples Learning objectives Derive \sum e_i f_i = n from the structure of \OL \otimes_\OK \OK/p Classify primes as split/inert/ramified in quadratic and cyclotomic fields Apply the identity to compute decomposition types from factorization data Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify \sum e_if_i = n for the factorization of (2) in \Z[i]. Answer: e=2, f=1, n=2: 2\cdot 1 = 2. \checkmark [Q2 (advanced).] Give a non-Galois cubic field where the primes above some p have differing e_i,f_i. Rubric: e.g.\ x^3-x-1; in a non-Galois extension e_i,f_i need not be constant across the primes above p, unlike the Galois case.

Core concepts The different ideal \mathfrakd_L/K and its relation to ramification The discriminant as the norm of the different Dedekind's theorem: p ramifies in L iff p \mid disc(L/K) Tame versus wild ramification Learning objectives Explain the relationship between the different, the discriminant, and ramification Derive Dedekind's ramification criterion from properties of the different Distinguish tame from wild ramification and identify which primes can be wildly ramified Historically hard. Why: notational overload (different vs.\ discriminant, ideal norm vs.\ field norm) compounds with a genuine abstraction jump into wild ramification, which has no analogue in the tame case. Mitigation: work tame ramification fully with explicit quadratic-field examples first; use a side-by-side table contrasting different vs.\ discriminant before stating Dedekind's theorem in general. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute disc(\Q(\sqrt d)) for squarefree d and identify the ramified primes. Answer: disc=d or 4d depending on d \bmod 4; ramified primes are exactly those dividing it. [Q2 (advanced).] Explain why wild ramification at p requires p \mid e, and construct an example. Rubric: tame ramification needs e coprime to the residue characteristic; \Q_p(p^1/p)/\Q_p via the Eisenstein polynomial x^p-p is totally, wildly ramified.

Core concepts Decomposition group D_P and inertia group I_P for P above p in Galois L/K Exact sequence 1 \to I_P \to D_P \to \Gal(k(P)/k(p)) \to 1 The Frobenius element/conjugacy class at unramified primes Statement of Chebotarev density, for motivation Learning objectives Derive the structure of D_P and I_P from the Galois action on primes above p Compute Frobenius elements in explicit Galois extensions Explain how Frobenius conjugacy classes encode splitting behavior Historically hard. Why: students must track three interacting group actions (the full Galois group, D_P, I_P) simultaneously, and the analogy with the residue field's Galois group is easy to lose. Mitigation: use one running example (e.g.\ \Q(\zeta_n)) throughout, with explicit subgroup-lattice diagrams at each step. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute D_P, I_P for a split, an inert, and a ramified prime in a quadratic field. Answer: split: D=I=1; inert: D=\Z/2, I=1; ramified: D=I=\Z/2. [Q2 (advanced).] Compute the Frobenius at p=2 in \Q(\zeta_7)/\Q and determine the splitting of 2. Rubric: order of 2 mod 7 is 3, so f=3; three unramified primes each with f=3.

readable_text: Weeks 5--9 (Sessions 9--18). Goal: develop local fields as the local counterpart to number fields, and connect local and global perspectives via places, Minkowski theory, and units.

Core concepts Global fields: number fields and function fields over finite fields, as a unifying perspective Places of a global field: archimedean and non-archimedean \OK's ideal theory recast in the global-field/local-field language used going forward Learning objectives Explain the analogy between number fields and function fields as global fields Enumerate the places of a given number field (real, complex, finite) Situate \OK's ideal theory within the local/global framework Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] List the places of \Q(i). Answer: one complex place (r_1=0, r_2=1); non-archimedean places correspond to primes of \Z[i]. [Q2 (advanced).] Compare places of F_q(t) with places of \Q, and identify the ``infinite place'' of F_q(t). Rubric: places of F_q(t) correspond to monic irreducibles plus the degree valuation at infinity; note the disanalogy that F_q(t) has no true archimedean place.

Core concepts Absolute values on a field; equivalence; Ostrowski's theorem for \Q Completion with respect to an absolute value; construction of \Qp \Zp as an inverse limit; p-adic expansions Learning objectives Prove Ostrowski's theorem classifying absolute values on \Q Construct \Qp both via completion and via inverse limits, and show these agree Apply p-adic expansions to solve concrete equations Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify |\cdot|_p satisfies the ultrametric inequality. Rubric: follows from additivity properties of the p-adic valuation v_p. [Q2 (advanced).] Does \sqrt 2 exist in \Q_7? If so, find its first three p-adic digits. Answer: 3^2 \equiv 2 \bmod 7, so by Hensel's lemma \sqrt 2 \in \Q_7; digits obtained by Hensel lifting.

Core concepts Hensel's Lemma and consequences (lifting roots, structure of \Zp^*) Uniqueness of the extension of an absolute value to a finite extension Unramified extensions \leftrightarrow residue field extensions; totally ramified extensions \leftrightarrow Eisenstein polynomials Structure theorem: every finite extension decomposes as unramified-then-totally-ramified Learning objectives Apply Hensel's Lemma to lift factorizations and determine unit structure Classify finite extensions of \Qp into unramified and totally ramified pieces Construct explicit local extensions via Eisenstein polynomials Historically hard. Why: the ``lifting'' intuition (a p-adic Newton's method) is unfamiliar, and holding the unramified/totally-ramified dichotomy in mind as two distinct extension mechanisms is easy to conflate. Mitigation: present Hensel's Lemma explicitly as p-adic Newton's method with a numerical example first, then build the dichotomy from two contrasting explicit extensions. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Use Hensel's Lemma to show \Zp^* contains all (p-1)-th roots of unity, p odd. Rubric: apply Hensel to x^p-1-1 using simple roots mod p from Fermat's little theorem. [Q2 (advanced).] Construct the unramified extension of \Qp of degree n, and contrast with \Qp(p^1/n). Rubric: unramified: adjoin roots of unity generating the degree-n residue field extension; ramified: Eisenstein polynomial x^n-p.

Core concepts Normalized absolute values at each place; the product formula \prod_v |x|_v = 1 Relating global ideal factorization to local completions K_v Weak approximation Learning objectives Prove the product formula for number fields Explain how localizing \OK at a prime recovers the local field K_v Apply weak approximation to construct elements with prescribed local behavior Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Verify \prod_v |2|_v = 1 for K = \Q. Answer: |2|_2 = 1/2, |2|_\infty = 2, all other |2|_v = 1; product =1. [Q2 (advanced).] Use the product formula to constrain elements of \OK that are small at every archimedean place and integral at every finite place. Rubric: the product formula forces a global product-of-one constraint; relate to Kronecker's theorem characterizing roots of unity.

Core concepts The Minkowski embedding K \hookrightarrow R^r_1\times C^r_2 and the lattice \OK Minkowski's convex body theorem The Minkowski bound; finiteness of Cl(K), completing Module 1 Learning objectives Derive the Minkowski bound and use it to compute class numbers in examples Prove finiteness of the ideal class group via the geometry of numbers Apply the Minkowski embedding to bound discriminants Historically hard. Why: this is a genuine change of category, from ideal-theoretic to geometric/volume-based reasoning, and the convex body theorem's soft counting argument is unlike the explicit proofs used so far. Mitigation: draw the 2-dimensional lattice picture for a real quadratic field before the general proof; give a step-by-step worked template for the Minkowski bound. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute the Minkowski bound for \Q(\sqrt-5) and determine the class number. Answer: bound \approx 2.85, so only p=2 needs checking, giving class number 2. [Q2 (advanced).] Prove Minkowski's convex body theorem. Rubric: pigeonhole argument on translates of half the body; volume exceeding the covolume forces overlap.

Core concepts The unit group \OK^*: torsion (roots of unity) and free part Statement: rank r_1 + r_2 - 1 The logarithmic embedding and the geometry-of-numbers proof strategy Learning objectives State and explain the structure of \OK^* via Dirichlet's unit theorem Derive the rank formula r_1+r_2-1 using the logarithmic embedding Compute fundamental units in small examples Historically hard. Why: the logarithmic embedding reuses the Minkowski-theory machinery in a new embedding, and bookkeeping the rank r_1+r_2-1 against the torsion kernel is a common source of off-by-one errors. Mitigation: work the rank computation for a real and an imaginary quadratic field side by side before the general proof. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Compute the unit rank of \Q(\sqrt2) and \Q(\sqrt-2), and find a fundamental unit for \Q(\sqrt2). Answer: ranks 1 and 0 respectively; fundamental unit 1+\sqrt2. [Q2 (advanced).] Derive r_1+r_2-1 from the logarithmic embedding \OK^*\to R^r_1+r_2. Rubric: image lies in a hyperplane by the product formula; discreteness plus boundedness gives a full-rank lattice in that hyperplane.

Core concepts The restricted direct product construction \prod'(K_v, O_v) The adèle ring \A_K as a restricted product over all places K embeds diagonally in \A_K; K is discrete (cocompactness stated, proved in \S3.2) Learning objectives Construct \A_K as a restricted direct product and verify it is a topological ring Explain why restricting to ``almost all O_v'' is necessary for local compactness Identify K as a discrete subring of \A_K Historically hard. Why: the restricted-product topology (``almost all coordinates in O_v'') is unlike any topology seen before this course. Mitigation: build up from finite sub-products (``S-adèles'') as a directed limit before taking the full restricted product. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show \prod'(\Q_p,\Zp) together with R is locally compact. Rubric: basic opens are products of opens at finitely many places times \prod \Zp elsewhere; local compactness follows from compactness of \Zp. [Q2 (advanced).] Show \Q embeds as a discrete subring of \A_\Q. Rubric: find a neighborhood of 0 meeting \Q only at 0, using that a rational number bounded archimedean and integral everywhere finite must be an integer.

Core concepts Local compactness of \A_K Pontryagin duality background (via the measure-theory prerequisite) Self-duality \A_K \cong \widehat\A_K via a nontrivial additive character Learning objectives Prove local compactness of \A_K from the restricted-product topology Explain the construction of self-duality via an additive character Apply Pontryagin duality formalism in the adelic setting Historically hard. Why: self-duality via a character is often presented too quickly, obscuring why the choice of character matters. Mitigation: construct the standard character on \A_\Q/\Q explicitly, local component by local component, before asserting self-duality in general. Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show \A_K/K is compact, given an explicit fundamental domain. Rubric: exhibit a compact fundamental domain as a product of bounded local pieces. [Q2 (advanced).] Construct \psi = \prod \psi_v on \A_\Q/\Q explicitly and verify it is nontrivial on \A_\Q but trivial on \Q. Rubric: \psi_\infty(x)=e^-2\pi i x, \psi_p(x)=e^2\pi i \x\_p; sum of fractional parts over all places is an integer.

Core concepts Idèles \A_K^* as units of \A_K, with their own finer restricted-product topology The idèle class group C_K = \A_K^*/K^* Relation between C_K and the classical ideal class group Cl(K) Learning objectives Explain why the idèle topology is strictly finer than the subspace topology from \A_K Derive the surjection from idèles to fractional ideals and identify its kernel Relate the idèle class group to the classical ideal class group Example questions [Q1 (foundational).] Show (x_v) \mapsto \prod P_v^v(x_v) is a surjective homomorphism from idèles to fractional ideals, and identify the kernel. Answer: kernel is the group of ``unit idèles.'' [Q2 (advanced).] Show C_K surjects onto Cl(K), and identify the kernel. Rubric: compose Q1's surjection with the quotient by principal ideals; kernel involves global units and archimedean components.

Core concepts The norm map |\cdot|: \A_K^* \to R_>0; norm-one idèles \A_K^1 Theorem: C_K^1 = \A_K^1/K^* is compact This single theorem encodes both finiteness of the class number and Dirichlet's unit theorem Learning objectives Prove compactness of C_K^1, building on Minkowski theory Explain how this theorem unifies finiteness of Cl(K) and the unit theorem Apply compactness to derive structural facts about C_K Historically hard. Answer: volume =1, matching d_\Q=1 up to normalization. [Q2 (advanced).] Express vol(\A_K/K) in terms of d_K for general K, and explain its role in Tate's thesis. Module 2 & $p$-adic computations, Hensel's Lemma applications, Minkowski bound and unit group computations & Weeks 5--9 & Tests the translation between local and global computations and geometry-of-numbers arguments, where reasoning errors typically surface \\
Module 3 & Adèle/idèle topology proofs, measure/volume computations, compactness argument write-ups & Weeks 10--12 & This material is proof-heavy and abstract; writing forces internalization of the topological/measure-theoretic arguments behind compactness \\
Module 4 & Local zeta integral computations; deriving the functional equation in worked cases (e.g.\ $K=\Q$) & Weeks 13--15 (contingent) & Since this module is only covered if time permits, homework is compressible and focuses on verifying the functional equation in the simplest nontrivial case as the essential takeaway \\
\bottomrule
